column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ṣakhr (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) say:

“What I have forbidden you, avoid it; and what I have commanded you, do of it what you are able. For what destroyed those before you was only their excessive questions and their disagreeing with their prophets.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
Fa-jtanibūhu (“avoid it”): keep away from it, obligatorily in what is unlawful and as a recommendation in what is disliked.
Fa-ʾtū minhu (“do of it”): obligatorily in what is obligatory and as a recommendation in what is recommended.
Istaṭaʿtum (“you are able”): you can manage.

Wa-khtilāfuhum (“and their disagreeing”): in the nominative, because this is more emphatic in censuring disagreement, since it is then not restricted to excessive disagreement as it would be if it were in the genitive. The meaning of disagreeing with the prophets is opposing them,
which entails the nation disagreeing among themselves.
The command to carry out what is commanded and avoid what is forbidden.

Prohibition is more stringent than command, because no allowance is made for committing any part of what is prohibited, whereas a command is restricted by ability. That is why one of the Salaf said: Righteous deeds are done by the righteous and the wicked alike, but sins are left only by one of true faith (ṣiddīq).

Inability to do an obligation, or part of it, removes the part one is unable to do, because Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. However, if what one is unable to do has a substitute and he does that, he has done what is due from him,

like someone unable to stand in prayer who moves to praying sitting or on his side. If he is unable to do the act of worship in the first place and so does not do it, like a sick person unable to fast, the duty of performing it is lifted while he is unable, and he must make it up afterwards.

Sometimes the obligation depends on ability only at the time it falls due, so if one is unable it is lifted altogether, like zakāt al-fiṭr for someone who does not have enough food for himself and his dependants.
The scholars have divided questions into two kinds. The first is asking in order to learn what one needs of the matters of the religion;

this is commanded, because of the saying of the Exalted, “So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know” [al-Naḥl 16:43]. The Companions' questions about the spoils of war, the kalālah [inheritance without parent or child] and other matters were of this kind.
The second is asking in order to cause difficulty and out of affectation, and this is what is forbidden.
A warning to this nation against opposing its Prophet, as happened with the nations before it.
